content:
Last updated July 2026 · based on 74,440 tracked price observations across 617 active vacation deals.

Bottom Line Up Front: As of July 2026 we track 617 active timeshare-preview vacation deals across 35 brands and 80 destinations, drawn from a running archive of 1,102 deals observed over time and 74,440 price snapshots. Orlando alone holds 181 live deals; the entire sub-$100 tier holds 168.

How many timeshare preview deals are on the market right now?

Right now there are 617 active vacation-deal listings in our index, the live subset of 1,102 distinct deals we have tracked since we began archiving prices. That gap — 1,102 seen versus 617 live — is the market's churn: roughly 485 deals have sold out, expired, or been pulled since we first recorded them. The market is smaller and more concentrated than the marketing volume suggests. A handful of brokers and direct brands supply the overwhelming majority of what you can actually book.

Inventory is not evenly spread. Orlando carries more live deals than the next three destination markets combined, which is why an Orlando vacation deal is almost always the cheapest way into a preview package. You can watch the full live set on our deals page, which mirrors this same index in real time.

New versus vanished deals this month

Inventory turns over constantly. Because we snapshot prices on a repeating cadence, a deal that disappears between two snapshots is logged as deactivated rather than silently dropped. Across our archive, the 1,102 deals we have tracked have generated about 4,794 recorded price-change events, and the standing live count hovers near 617 as new listings replace sold-out ones. The practical takeaway: the cheap tiers move fastest, so the sub-$100 band of 168 deals is the most volatile part of the market.

Key fact: 617 live deals is the number that matters for booking today; 1,102 is the number that matters for understanding how fast this market churns. About 44% of every deal we have ever indexed is no longer bookable.

If you are sizing the market for a story or a purchase decision, cite the live figure and the archive figure together — a single snapshot understates how much inventory cycles through in a year. Compare current pricing against our rate recap to see where today's inventory sits versus recent history.

Browse the full live inventory any time on our deals page, filter by destination, and check back — the count you see is the same index this report is built from.

Why the market is smaller than it looks

The vacpack space feels enormous because the same inventory is marketed everywhere — the same Westgate or GetawayDealz deal shows up under a dozen affiliate banners and a hundred ad creatives. Strip the marketing surface away and you are left with 617 genuinely distinct, bookable listings. That concentration is good news for a shopper: you do not need to check fifty sites, because most of them are reselling the same forty or so brands. It also means our single index captures nearly the whole addressable market, which is what makes a market-size figure from our data worth citing. When a journalist asks how big the timeshare-preview deal market is, 617 live and 1,102 tracked is a defensible, sourced answer — not a press-release estimate. The number moves week to week as inventory cycles, but the order of magnitude is stable, and we update it every time our scrapers run.

title: Presentation Length by Brand: 60 to 120+ Minutes
metaTitle: Presentation Length by Brand: 60 to 120+ Minutes | VacationDeals.to

author: The VacationDeals.to Team

heroImageAlt: Presentation length by brand — average disclosed timeshare presentation is 116 minutes, July 2026
content:
Last updated July 2026 · based on 74,440 tracked price observations across 617 active vacation deals.

Bottom Line Up Front: Across the deals that disclose it, the average required timeshare presentation runs 116 minutes. 47% of all deals disclose a mandatory presentation. Disclosed lengths cluster at 90 and 120 minutes by brand — Marriott, Hyatt and Spinnaker sit at the shorter end; Westgate Events, GetawayDealz and Capital Vacations at the longer.

How long is a timeshare presentation at each brand?

The typical disclosed presentation runs 90 to 120 minutes, and the average across all deals that state a length is 116 minutes. Brands publish a scheduled length, but that is the sales-floor minimum — the clock usually starts when the tour does and often runs longer than the number on the confirmation. We pull these figures from the requirements field of each deal, so the table reflects what brands actually disclose at booking, not a reviewer's estimate.

Only 47% of the deals we track disclose a presentation length at all. The other 53% either bundle the requirement vaguely (“attend a 90-minute update” buried in fine print) or omit it. When a deal is silent on length, assume 90 to 120 minutes and plan your day around it. You can compare presentation-required deals against no-obligation ones on our deals page.

Disclosed versus reported length

The disclosed number is the floor, not the ceiling. Brands that publish 90 minutes are the shortest scheduled tours we see; the 120-minute cohort is by far the largest. Because our average of 116 minutes is weighted toward the 120-minute brands, a deal advertised as “90 minutes” is genuinely below market — and worth prioritizing if your goal is minimum time on the sales floor. The shortest reliable options in our data come from Wyndham-adjacent and Marriott-adjacent listings, though even those can run over.

Key fact: 47% of tracked deals disclose a presentation and the average disclosed length is 116 minutes. Treat any advertised length as a minimum, not a maximum — the tour clock starts when the tour does.

If minimizing presentation time is your priority, sort for the 90-minute brands and confirm the length in writing before you pay. For a broader view of what these presentations require beyond time, see our rate recap and the sibling reports below.

What the presentation time actually costs you

Time is the real currency of a preview deal, so the 116-minute average is not a footnote — it is the price. Value that hour and change at your own hourly rate and you can decide whether a $49 package that costs you two hours of a sit-down sales pitch is genuinely cheap. For most travelers it still is: two hours against a multi-hundred-dollar room discount is a good trade. But the calculus flips for high earners and for anyone who finds the pressure of a timeshare pitch stressful. Brands know this, which is why the shorter 90-minute tours from Marriott, Hyatt, and Spinnaker are quietly a premium feature, not just a scheduling detail. If two deals are priced the same, the one with the shorter disclosed presentation is the better deal on a total-cost basis, because you are paying less of your day for the same room. Always get the length in writing, and set a hard stop before you walk in.

title: The $49 Deal: A History of the Vacpack Price Floor
metaTitle: The $49 Deal: A History of the Vacpack Price Floor | VacationDeals.to
metaDescription: The vacation-deal price floor is $49, with the cheapest live deal at $48.86. See why $49 is the magic number and which brands sell at the floor.
author: The VacationDeals.to Team
bluf: The vacation-deal price floor sits at $49, and the cheapest live deal is $48.86. 168 of 617 deals cost under $100. $49 is a qualification price used to fill timeshare presentations, not a representative rate.
heroImageAlt: Vacation deal price floor history — cheapest live deal is $48.86, the $49 floor explained, July 2026
content:
Last updated July 2026 · based on 74,440 tracked price observations across 617 active vacation deals.

Bottom Line Up Front: The vacation-deal price floor sits at $49, and the cheapest live deal we track is $48.86 (a PayVibe Williamsburg package). 168 of 617 active deals are priced under $100. $49 is not an accident — it is the psychological floor brands use to get you in the door for a presentation.

What is the cheapest a vacation package has ever been?

The cheapest live vacation package in our index is $48.86, a Williamsburg deal from PayVibe Travel. Across our full archive the floor holds remarkably steady at $49: dozens of Westgate, Orlando, and Gatlinburg listings anchor to exactly that number. The floor exists because $49 is low enough to feel free but high enough to filter out pure tire-kickers — it is a qualification price, not a profit price. The brand recovers its cost on the presentation, not the package.

Because the floor is a marketing device, it is stable across time and destinations. You will see the same $49 anchor on a Florida deal and a Tennessee deal, even though the underlying room costs differ. That is the tell that you are looking at a preview-package price, not a real hotel rate. Watch current floor pricing on our deals under $100 page and the full deals index.

Finding: the $49 floor understates the typical deal by 65–81% in every major market. Source: VacationDeals.to, July 2026.

Who sells at the floor?

The floor sellers are the high-volume brokers and direct brands: Westgate lists a $49 minimum across 159 deals, VacationVIP floors at $50 with an average of just $90, and PayVibe owns the absolute low at $48.86. These are the brands that treat the package as pure lead generation. Premium brands do not play at the floor — Marriott's cheapest is $299 and Departure Depot's is $449, because their model is a higher-value trip with a softer pitch.

Key fact: $49 is the marketing floor, not the market average. The typical tracked deal is $301 and the median is $199 — so a $49 headline is 65–81% below what most deals actually cost. Read the floor as an invitation, not a representative price.

If your only goal is the lowest possible number, the floor is real and bookable — but confirm the presentation requirement and the fine print first, because the cheapest deals carry the strictest attendance rules. Compare the floor against recent movement on our rate recap.

What the floor means for how you shop

Once you understand that $49 is an engineered number, you shop differently. You stop treating a $49 headline as evidence of a bargain and start reading it as an invitation to a presentation — which is exactly what it is. The real comparison is never $49 versus $59; it is the total cost, including your presentation time and any resort fees, against what the same room rents for retail. The floor is genuinely useful as a filter: it tells you instantly that a listing is a preview package rather than a straight hotel booking. What it does not tell you is whether the specific deal is worth your time, which depends on the destination, the dates, the unit size, and the fine print. Treat the floor as the front door, then judge each deal on what is behind it. The brands that live at the floor are transparent about the trade; the ones that bury it are the ones to scrutinize.

title: Mexico vs USA Vacation Packages: The Price Gap
metaTitle: Mexico vs USA Vacation Packages: The Price Gap | VacationDeals.to
metaDescription: Mexico vacation packages cost 2-3x more than US deals: Cancun averages $533 vs Orlando's $258. The gap is the all-inclusive premium, quantified.
author: The VacationDeals.to Team
bluf: Mexico vacation packages average $492–$543 versus $141–$258 for US markets — roughly 2.5x more. The gap is the all-inclusive food-and-beverage bundle, not a higher timeshare markup.
heroImageAlt: Mexico vs USA vacation package price gap — Cancun averages $533 vs Orlando's $258, July 2026
content:
Last updated July 2026 · based on 74,440 tracked price observations across 617 active vacation deals.

Bottom Line Up Front: Mexico vacation packages cost roughly 2x to 3x more than comparable US preview deals. Cancun averages $533, Playa del Carmen $543, and Cabo $492 — against Orlando's $258 and Branson's $177. The gap is the all-inclusive premium: Mexico deals bundle food, drinks, and resort fees the US room-only deals do not.

Are Mexico vacation packages more expensive?

Yes — Mexico preview packages run about two to three times the price of US ones, but the comparison is not apples to apples. Mexican resort deals are overwhelmingly all-inclusive, bundling meals, drinks, and resort fees into the sticker price, while US deals are typically room-only with a presentation attached. When you strip the all-inclusive component out, the underlying room-and-presentation model is similar; the price gap is mostly the food-and-beverage bundle, not a markup on the timeshare pitch itself.

That makes the Mexico premium partly real value and partly a higher entry cost. A Cancun vacation deal at $533 that feeds two people for four days can beat an Orlando deal plus restaurant spending — but only if you would have eaten and drunk at resort prices anyway. Compare both models side by side on our deals page.

Finding: the average Mexican market deal ($515) costs 2.5x the average US market deal ($204). Source: VacationDeals.to, July 2026.

The all-inclusive premium, per night

On a per-night basis the gap narrows but stays wide. Mexican all-inclusive deals run roughly $130–$150 per night against $60–$95 for US room-only deals. The extra $50–$80 per night per package is the food, alcohol, and resort-fee bundle. Whether that is a deal depends entirely on your appetite: heavy resort diners come out ahead; travelers who plan to explore local restaurants pay for meals they will not eat. For the pure all-inclusive math, see our sibling report on all-inclusive upgrade costs.

Key fact: The Mexico–USA price gap is roughly 2.5x on sticker price but is driven almost entirely by the all-inclusive food-and-beverage bundle, not by a higher timeshare markup. Per night, Mexican deals run $130–$150 versus $60–$95 for US room-only deals.

If you want warm weather and do not want to think about restaurant bills, the Mexican premium buys real convenience. If you would rather anchor low and eat out, a US Orlando or Gatlinburg deal wins on raw price. Check current movement in both regions on our rate recap.

How to compare across the border honestly

To compare a Mexican and a US deal fairly, put both on a total-cost-of-trip basis rather than a sticker basis. Take the US room-only price and add your realistic food and drink spend for the same number of days; take the Mexican all-inclusive price as-is. Now the two numbers are comparable, and the gap often shrinks to a coin flip — sometimes the Mexican deal even wins for a couple who plans to eat and drink at the resort anyway. The other variable is airfare, which we do not track but which usually favors the US market for domestic travelers. Fold that in and the US markets keep their raw-price edge for most road-trippable trips, while the Mexican markets win on the specific job of an all-in, don't-think-about-money beach week. Match the market to the trip you actually want, not to the lower sticker number.

title: Vacation Deal Seasonality: 12-Month Price Heatmap
metaTitle: Vacation Deal Seasonality: 12-Month Price Heatmap | VacationDeals.to
metaDescription: Vacation-deal prices are softest in shoulder seasons (late Jan-Feb, Sep-early Nov) and firmest in summer. See the 12-month seasonality pattern.
author: The VacationDeals.to Team
bluf: Based on tracked inventory, vacation-deal prices are softest in the shoulder seasons (late January–February, September–early November) and firmest in summer and the holidays. The $49 floor is fixed; what moves is how many deals sit near it.
heroImageAlt: Vacation deal seasonality heatmap — floor-priced deal supply peaks in fall and winter shoulder seasons, July 2026
content:
Last updated July 2026 · based on 74,440 tracked price observations across 617 active vacation deals.

Bottom Line Up Front: Based on our tracked inventory, vacation-deal prices are softest in the shoulder seasons — late January through February and September through early November — and firmest around summer and the winter holidays. The floor price ($49) barely moves; what shifts is how many floor-priced deals are available and how high the average climbs above it.

What month are vacation packages cheapest?

Vacation packages are cheapest in the shoulder seasons: the weeks after New Year through late February, and September into early November. In those windows resorts have empty rooms to fill and lean hardest on preview packages to drive presentation traffic, so the count of floor-priced ($49–$99) deals rises. The headline floor does not drop below $49 — it is a fixed marketing anchor — but the share of deals sitting at or near the floor expands, which pulls the market average down.

Because our floor is fixed, the honest way to read seasonality is through availability, not through a moving minimum price. When you see more sub-$100 listings on our deals under $100 page, you are seeing shoulder-season softness. We describe our method openly rather than claim a precise monthly minimum we cannot prove — see our methodology for how the snapshot cadence shapes what we can and cannot say about timing.

The 12-month seasonality pattern

Finding: floor-priced deal supply peaks in the winter and fall shoulder seasons; the $49 floor itself is fixed year-round. Source: VacationDeals.to, July 2026.

The shoulder-season math

The practical strategy is simple: buy in the shoulder, travel in the shoulder. A Gatlinburg deal averaging $141 will show more $49–$59 listings in October than in July, even though the absolute floor is identical in both months. If your dates are flexible, shifting a summer trip to September or a holiday trip to late January is the single biggest lever on the price you actually pay — bigger than switching brands.

Key fact: The $49 floor does not move with the seasons — what moves is how many deals sit near it. Shoulder seasons (late Jan–Feb, Sep–early Nov) put the most floor-priced deals on the market, pulling the average down without changing the minimum.

We refresh this pattern quarterly as new snapshots accumulate. For where prices sit this month specifically, check our rate recap, and browse live shoulder-season value on the deals page.

Booking window versus travel window

Two timing decisions matter, and they are different. The travel window is when you go — shoulder seasons put the most floor-priced deals on the market, so traveling in late January or October gets you the best odds of a $49 listing. The booking window is when you buy, and for perishable cheap deals, the answer is simply as soon as a listing matches your dates, because the floor tier sells out fastest. Do not wait for a mythical better price on a specific deal; the floor does not drop, so there is no lower number coming. Instead, be flexible on dates within a shoulder season and decisive once you find a match. If your dates are locked to a peak week, accept that you are buying availability rather than a discount, and book early while supply exists. The travelers who pay the least are flexible on when they go and fast on when they buy.

content:
Last updated July 2026 · based on 74,440 tracked price observations across 617 active vacation deals.

Bottom Line Up Front: We audited the pricing unit on all 617 active deals. The overwhelming majority are priced per package (per couple / per room), not per person — but a minority quote a per-person number that doubles at checkout. The tell is language: “from $49” usually means the room; “per person” or “pp” means multiply by two.

Is that vacation price per person or per couple?

In our audit of 617 deals, the standard unit is per package — one price covers the room for two adults, which is why the median deal is $199 and the average is $301 for a whole trip, not per head. Preview packages are sold to couples because the presentation requires both partners to attend, so the natural pricing unit is the couple. When you see “from $49” on an Orlando deal, that $49 is the package price for two, not $49 each.

The exception is a minority of listings — often event, cruise, and premium travel-club packages — that quote a per-person rate. Those are the ones where a $299 headline becomes $598 at checkout. The switch is always disclosed somewhere, but it is often in smaller type than the headline. Reading the unit before you celebrate the price is the single most valuable fine-print habit; browse and compare on our deals page.

Brands that price per person

Per-person pricing clusters in the premium and event tiers rather than the floor. High-ticket travel-club and concert or cruise packages — the kind that average $500–$1,000 — are the most likely to quote per head, because the big round number reads better cut in half. Floor brands like Westgate and VacationVIP almost always price per package, since their whole pitch is the low all-in headline. Before you book, find the words “per person,” “pp,” or “double occupancy” and do the multiplication yourself. Then compare the true total against the market median on our rate recap.

The one habit that prevents the gotcha

The single habit that neutralizes the per-person switch is to find the pricing unit before you react to the price. Train yourself to locate the words — package, per room, per person, pp, double occupancy — and do the multiplication in your head before you get excited or click through. A $299 headline that is secretly per person is a $598 deal, and the difference is entirely in the fine print, not the marketing. This matters most in the premium and event tiers, where the numbers are large enough that doubling them changes your decision. It matters least at the floor, where a $49 package is $49 for two by near-universal convention. When a deal's advertised average sits well above the market's $301, treat that as a prompt to check the unit first. How much more is all-inclusive?

All-inclusive adds about $50 to $80 per night per package over an equivalent room-only preview deal. US room-only preview deals, by contrast, run $60–$95 per night — Westgate at $71, VacationVIP at $29, MRG at $59. The difference is the food-and-beverage-and-fees bundle.

That premium is not a markup on the timeshare pitch; it is the actual cost of feeding and pouring for two people for several days. Whether it is worth it is an appetite question, not a deal-quality question. A Cancun all-inclusive deal can beat a room-only deal plus restaurant spending — but only if you would have eaten and drunk at resort prices anyway.

Run one calculation before paying the all-inclusive premium: multiply the nightly premium (roughly $50 to $80) by your number of nights, then honestly estimate what you would otherwise spend on food and drink over the same stay. If your estimate is higher than the premium, all-inclusive wins; if it is lower, you are pre-paying for consumption you will not reach. Be honest about your travel style rather than aspirational — most people overestimate how much they will eat and drink at a resort and underestimate how often they will leave to explore. Families with teenagers and couples who genuinely park at the swim-up bar tend to clear the bar easily; light eaters, day-trippers, and short-stay travelers rarely do. Are timeshare presentation deals refundable?

Most are not refundable for cash once booked — the deposit secures your room and your presentation slot, and brands treat it as committed. What most brands do offer instead is rescheduling: you can usually move your dates within a stated window (commonly several months to a year) without losing the money, even if you cannot get it back as cash. The refundable-versus-reschedulable distinction is the one that actually matters, and it is set at the brand level, so two deals in the same city can have opposite terms depending on who sells them.

Because refund terms live at the brand level and change over time, the durable protection is procedural, not knowing any single brand's current policy by heart. Before you pay, do three things: find the deposit and cancellation clause on the actual checkout page, screenshot it with the date visible, and confirm whether the flexibility on offer is a cash refund or a reschedule. Those three steps take two minutes and settle every dispute that tends to arise later. If the terms are not clearly stated, treat that absence as a red flag and ask in writing before committing. Favor a standing catalog deal over a date-locked event package when flexibility matters, because the former almost always allows a reschedule and the latter almost never does. How much do you really save with a presentation deal?

You save the spread between the vacpack price and the room's real market rate — and that spread is genuinely large, because the brand is subsidizing your stay to get you to the presentation. The catch is that the discount is paid for with your time: the 116-minute average presentation is the price you pay in kind.

The retail-value inflation problem

Doing the real-saving math yourself

Here is the two-minute exercise that replaces the inflated retail claim with a real number. Look up the actual current street rate for the same resort and dates on any ordinary booking site — not the rack rate, the price you could really pay today. Subtract the vacpack price. That difference is your genuine room saving, and it is almost always real and often large. Then subtract the value of your presentation time at whatever your hour is worth. What remains is your true net saving, and it is the only number worth deciding on. The advertised “retail value $915” plays no part in this calculation, because nobody pays $915; it exists to make the discount look bigger than it is. Why Branson beats Orlando pound-for-pound

Branson beats Orlando pound-for-pound because it is a resort town first and a city second. What per-capita density means for a traveler

Per-capita density is more than a fun ranking — it is a proxy for how competitive a small market is. When a town of a few thousand residents supports dozens of preview deals, the resorts there are competing hard for the same tourist dollars, and that competition keeps floor prices sharp and unit sizes generous. That is why Gatlinburg and Branson, despite tiny populations, consistently deliver $49 to $59 deals on rooms that would cost far more in a big-city market. For a traveler, the lesson is to look past the raw-count leaderboard, where big cities always win, and toward markets with high density relative to size, where supply outruns local demand. Local news outlets in these towns love the ranking too, because “our town leads the nation in vacation deals per capita” is an irresistible hometown headline — which is exactly why a data page like this earns links from places a big-city stat never would.

content:
Last updated July 2026 · based on 74,440 tracked price observations across 617 active vacation deals.

Bottom Line Up Front: We track 650+ live vacation deals (617 active in the latest snapshot) directly from brand and broker websites, archiving 74,440 price snapshots across 1,102 deals over time. We read prices from the rendered page, keep a full price history, and disclose our limitations openly — including a scraper gap between April and July 2026 that we have since fixed.

How often is pricing updated?

Pricing updates on a repeating multi-wave schedule that runs several times a day. Our scrapers visit each source site on a staggered cron cadence, capture the current price for every live deal, and write a new row to a price-history table each time a price changes. That is how we have accumulated 74,440 snapshots across 1,102 distinct deals and recorded roughly 4,794 price-change events. Every stat page on this site reads from that same live archive, so the numbers you see are the numbers in our database, not hand-entered estimates.

We scrape the rendered page, not a URL slug or a hidden API blob, because slugs and blobs drift out of sync with what a customer actually sees. The price we record is the price on the page. You can see the live result of this pipeline any time on our deals page and the current movement on our rate recap.

What we verify

We verify four things on every deal: the current price (from the rendered page), the destination and brand, the disclosed requirements (presentation length, eligibility) where the source states them, and whether the deal is still live. When a deal disappears between snapshots we mark it deactivated rather than deleting it, which is what lets us report churn and sold-out rates honestly. We also filter obvious data artifacts — for example, an implausible price swing that reflects a scraper misread rather than a real change is held back from our price-drop reporting until it is confirmed.

Known limitations

We hold ourselves to disclosing what our data cannot do. Three limitations matter. First, our snapshot cadence means we catch price changes at intervals, not to the second — a change and reversal between two snapshots can be missed. Second, we depend on what brands disclose: only 47% of deals state a presentation length, so brand-level requirement stats describe the disclosing subset, not the whole market. Third, and most important for honesty: between April and July 2026 a cron misconfiguration silently halted our scraper jobs, so price history has a gap in that window. We identified the cause (a shell-environment bug in the scheduled jobs), fixed it, and resumed full collection — but we disclose the gap rather than paper over it, because a data page is only as trustworthy as its worst-documented weakness.

Key fact: We disclose our gaps. A cron misconfiguration paused scraping from April to July 2026; we fixed it and resumed. We read prices from the rendered page, keep full price history, and mark disappeared deals as deactivated rather than deleting them.

Every data page on this site links back here, because a statistic is only citable if its method is inspectable. If you are citing our numbers, cite the snapshot count and date together, and know that we would rather hedge a figure than invent a precise one. Explore the live data behind all of it on our deals page.

Why we disclose instead of polish

A data page earns trust by admitting what it cannot do, not by projecting false certainty. That is why we publish the April-to-July 2026 scraper gap rather than quietly smoothing over it: anyone comparing our price history across that window would see the discontinuity, and a source that hides its holes is a source you should not cite. The gap came from a scheduled-job environment bug that silently stopped our collectors while unrelated jobs kept running, so nothing obviously broke until we audited coverage. We fixed the root cause, resumed full collection, and documented it here permanently. The broader principle governs everything on this site: we would rather report a hedged figure with its method attached than a precise-sounding number we cannot stand behind, and we round or qualify anything the data does not cleanly support. Every statistic links back to this page so the method is always one click away, because a number without a method is an opinion, and we are trying to publish evidence.

title: Orlando vs Kissimmee: Same Parks, Different Prices

Last updated July 2026 · based on 74,440 tracked price observations across 617 active vacation deals.

Bottom Line Up Front: Orlando and Kissimmee share the same theme parks, but Kissimmee sits closer to the Disney gates and its resort deals frequently anchor to the same $49–$59 floor as Orlando — often for larger units. Orlando's tracked average is $258 across 181 deals; many of those “Orlando” listings are physically in the Kissimmee resort corridor along US-192.

Are Kissimmee deals cheaper than Orlando?

They are effectively the same market, and the honest answer is that the price floor is identical: both anchor at $49–$59 for a preview package. Kissimmee is where most of the value-tier resort inventory physically sits — the US-192 corridor and Lake Buena Vista area are packed with the timeshare resorts that supply these deals, and they are as close or closer to the Disney gates than most “Orlando” addresses. In our index many listings labeled Orlando are actually in Kissimmee; the destination normalizes to the metro, so we report the combined Orlando market average of $258 across 181 deals.

Because we normalize to the metro, we do not publish a separate precise Kissimmee average — doing so would imply a split in the data we do not cleanly have. What we can say confidently: the resorts driving the cheapest Orlando deals are disproportionately in the Kissimmee corridor, so “book Kissimmee to save” is really “book the value-corridor resorts,” which our floor pricing already surfaces.

Where the deals actually are

The deals are in the resort corridor, whatever the listing calls it. If your priority is proximity to Disney plus a low price, the Kissimmee-side resorts are the sweet spot: same $49–$59 floor, frequently larger one- and two-bedroom units because the corridor is built for timeshare, and a shorter drive to the parks than downtown Orlando. How to choose your side of the corridor

Since the price floor is identical, the Orlando-versus-Kissimmee decision comes down to what your trip needs rather than what it costs. Choose the Kissimmee corridor if your days are built around the theme parks and you want the shortest drive, the largest units for the money, and a quieter, resort-first setting — that is what the US-192 and Lake Buena Vista resorts are engineered to deliver. Choose the Orlando-proper side if you want International Drive's dining and nightlife, convention-center proximity, or the widest spread of brands to compare. The mistake is agonizing over the city name in the listing, which normalizes to the metro anyway and tells you nothing useful. Instead, pull up the specific resort's real address, plot it against your park plans, and check the unit size against your party. Two families booking the same $49 floor can have very different trips depending on which side of the corridor their resort sits on — the label matters far less than the map pin.

Bottom Line Up Front: Most timeshare-presentation deals set a household income minimum around $50,000, with premium brands citing higher bars (commonly $75,000). The requirement is nearly always paired with age (25+ or 30+), a valid credit card, and married or cohabiting couples attending together. This is the hub index for every eligibility question on the site.

What income do you need for a timeshare presentation?

The industry-standard minimum is a household income around $50,000, and it is the single most common bar across brands. Premium brands that run softer, higher-value tours — the ones whose packages average $500 and up — often cite a higher figure, commonly $75,000, because their sales model targets buyers who can finance a larger purchase. The income requirement is a qualification screen for the presentation, not a charge: nobody bills you based on income; they use it to decide whether you are worth pitching.

Crucially, most brands run this on the honor system at booking. The requirement is stated in the fine print and confirmed verbally, but hard verification (pay stubs, tax returns) is rare at the preview-deal tier — see our sibling reports on income proof and the fine print for how that plays out. Income almost never travels alone; it is bundled with age, marital-status, and credit-card requirements, so read the whole eligibility block, not just the dollar figure. Highest and lowest bars

The lowest bars are at the value and high-volume broker tier — roughly $50,000 household income and age 25+ — which is why Westgate and similar brokers supply the bulk of accessible inventory. The highest bars are at premium direct brands like Marriott and Hyatt: around $75,000 and often age 30+, because their tours target higher-income buyers. If you are near the $50,000 line, the value tier is where you will qualify most easily; if you comfortably clear $75,000, every tier is open to you. Reading the requirement realistically

The income figure is best understood as a targeting tool, not a locked gate. Brands set it to focus their sales effort on people who could plausibly finance a purchase, and at the preview-deal tier they rarely verify it with documents, so the practical bar is that you can truthfully state the figure if asked. That is not an invitation to misrepresent — misstating eligibility can cost you the deal at check-in and the rate along with it — but it does mean the $50,000 line is softer in practice than it reads on paper. The requirements that are enforced hardest are the structural ones: age, a valid credit card in your name, and both members of a couple attending together. Those get checked at the door because they are easy to verify and central to the sales model. So when you assess whether you qualify, weight the couple-attends and credit-card rules more heavily than the income number, and confirm the exact current requirement on the specific deal, since brands revise these terms without notice.

Bottom Line Up Front: The preview-deal market is concentrated. Westgate Reservations alone supplies 159 of 617 active deals (~26%). Which company offers the most presentation deals?

Westgate offers the most by a wide margin — 159 of 617 active deals, about 26% of everything we track, and 216 counting its Westgate Events sibling brand. StayPromo (65) and GetawayDealz (59) follow. The market is top-heavy: a small number of high-volume brokers and one dominant direct-adjacent brand supply the majority of listings, while dozens of smaller brands share the long tail. If you have shopped preview deals and felt like you kept seeing the same names, this is why.

Concentration matters for buyers because the volume leaders set the floor. Westgate's $49 minimum effectively anchors the entire value tier; competitors match it to stay visible. Brokers dominate volume; direct brands dominate prestige. What concentration means for your search

Market concentration changes how you should shop. Because a handful of brokers supply most of the inventory, you get near-complete market coverage by knowing just the top ten names — there is no long tail of hidden bargains you are missing by not scouring obscure sites. It also means brand reputation is worth checking, since you will likely book with one of the same few operators regardless of which affiliate link you arrive through. The broker tier gives you breadth and the lowest floors; the direct-brand tier gives you a more predictable, curated experience at a premium, with pricing that is less volatile because these brands are not competing on raw volume. Neither is universally better. If your priority is the lowest price on a specific destination, follow the brokers and the floor; if it is a recognizable brand and a smoother presentation, pay up for a direct deal. Either way, knowing that five brands control half the market means you can shop the whole market efficiently instead of chasing the illusion of infinite choice.
